items.title: 3.6.1 Molecular orbital diagrams of some diatomic molecules and their bond orders

source_refs.note: Topic 3.6.1, printed pages 65-67 (Figures 3.36 to 3.38), with the bond orders of He2, N2 and O2.

blocks.text: The electron configuration of He is 1s². For a successful formation of He₂ molecule, 1s orbitals of two He atoms must combine to form bonding (δ1s) and anti-bonding (δ*1s) orbitals as shown in Figure 3.36. Out of four electrons, two enter the bonding molecular orbital δ (1s) and the remaining two occupy the antibonding δ*(1s) molecular orbital. But on calculation we discover that the bond order for He₂ is zero. Hence, He₂ molecule is not formed.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The print uses δ (delta) where σ (sigma) is meant. Two 1s orbitals give the bonding σ1s and the anti-bonding σ*1s molecular orbitals, as Figure 3.36 shows.

blocks.alt: Energy arrow on the left. 2He = 1s with a pair of electrons on each side, each tagged A.O. In the middle, sigma* (1s) above, tagged A.B.M.O, and sigma (1s) below, tagged B.M.O, each holding a pair of opposite arrows.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.36: Molecular orbital diagram of He2 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.36).

blocks.text: The molecular orbital diagram of N₂ based on this electron configuration is shown in the figure below (Figure. 3.37). The valence shell 2s on both N atoms give σ2s and σ*2s orbitals; whereas, 2p orbitals give six molecular orbitals which are arranged in the increasing order of energy as:

blocks.text_alt: σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2sPx

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The last orbital is printed σ*2sPx; it is the anti-bonding σ*2px orbital: σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px.
The bond order for N₂ can be calculated from its orbital diagram as:
Therefore, there are three covalent bonds between the nitrogen atoms in this molecule. One of these is a σ bond while the other two are π bonds. Nitrogen molecule has a triple bond between its atoms.

Molecular orbitals from bottom: pi(2py) and pi(2pz) each with a pair, sigma(2px) with a pair (B.M.O); pi*(2py), pi*(2pz) and sigma*(2px) empty (A.B.M.O). Lower part: 7N = 2s with a pair on each side (A.O), sigma(2s) with a pair (B.M.O) and sigma*(2s) with a pair (A.B.M.O).

blocks.text: The formation of molecular orbitals in oxygen molecule is shown as follows in figure 36.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: There is no figure 36; the molecular orbital diagram of the oxygen molecule is Figure 3.38.
The bond energy of the MOs can be arranged as

blocks.text_alt: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2px < π2py = π2pz < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px

blocks.text: The bond order of oxygen is 2 ((6 − 2)/2), which shows the presence of one σ and one π bond between the oxygen atoms, i.e. they are linked by a double bond (O=O). Oxygen molecule is paramagnetic in nature, which means it is attracted by a magnetic field. Paramagnetic substances have one or more unpaired electrons in them. A substance with large number of unpaired electrons is strongly paramagnetic. MOT successfully explains the paramagnetic behavior of oxygen molecule.
Liquid oxygen is attracted and gets suspended between the poles of a strong magnet.

The MO diagram of oxygen shows the presence of two unpaired electrons, one in π*(2py) and π*(2pz) each. Due to the presence of these unpaired electrons, oxygen molecule has a net magnetic field, which interacts with the external magnetic field.

Molecular orbitals from bottom: sigma(2px) with a pair, pi(2py) and pi(2pz) each with a pair (B.M.O); pi*(2py) and pi*(2pz) with one up arrow each and sigma*(2px) empty (A.B.M.O). Lower part: 8O = 2s pairs (A.O), sigma(2s) and sigma*(2s) each with a pair.
